problems.name: Ryser's conjecture on covers of r-partite hypergraphs
problems.field: Extremal hypergraph theory; covers and matchings
problems.statement:
An $r$-partite $r$-uniform hypergraph $H$ has disjoint vertex parts $V_1,\ldots,V_r$ and every edge has exactly one vertex in each part. Let $	au(H)$ be its covering number (least size of a vertex set meeting every edge) and $
u(H)$ its matching number. Ryser's conjecture asserts $	au(H)\le(r-1)
u(H)$. For $r=2$ this is Konig's theorem; Aharoni proved $r=3$; in the intersecting case ($
u=1$) it was known through $r=5$ (Gyarfas, Tuza), and truncated projective planes show it would be tight whenever $r-1$ is a prime power. Does every $r$-partite $r$-uniform hypergraph satisfy $	au(H)\le(r-1)
u(H)$?
problems.posedBy: Herbert J. Ryser (attributed); an equivalent formulation appears in J. R. Henderson's 1971 Caltech thesis
problems.ageNote: Year of Henderson's thesis, the earliest written source the manuscripts cite; they point to Best and Wanless, 'What did Ryser conjecture?' (2018), for the history of the attribution.
problems.resultNote: Ryser's conjecture is false, already for intersecting hypergraphs. September 23: for every sufficiently large prime $s\equiv2\pmod3$ and every sufficiently large odd $n$ (threshold depending on $s$), there is an intersecting $(s^n+1)$-partite $(s^n+1)$-uniform hypergraph with $\tau=s^n+1$, against the conjectured $s^n$. September 27: for every sufficiently large prime $q$, an intersecting $(q+1)$-partite $(q+1)$-uniform hypergraph with $\tau=q+1$ and exactly $q+1$ nonisolated vertices in each part. Not given: an explicit rank or example, or anything for small $r$ (cases $r=4,5$ remain open in general).

problems.name: Gottschalk's surjunctivity conjecture
problems.field: Symbolic dynamics on groups; cellular automata
problems.statement: For a group $G$ and a finite alphabet $A$, a cellular automaton on $A^G$ is a map $\tau(x)(g)=\phi((x(gu))_{u\in M})$ given by a finite memory set $M\subset G$ and a local rule $\phi:A^M\to A$. $G$ is surjunctive if every injective cellular automaton on $A^G$, for every finite $A$, is surjective. Gromov and Weiss proved that sofic groups are surjunctive, and surjunctivity implies Kaplansky's direct finiteness over finite fields. Gottschalk (1973) conjectured that every group is surjunctive. Is every group surjunctive?
problems.posedBy: Walter Gottschalk, Some general dynamical notions, Recent Advances in Topological Dynamics, LNM 318 (1973)
problems.resultNote: The group $G$ and elements $a,b\in K[G]$ of the characteristic-two direct-finiteness counterexample ($K$ finite, $G$ finitely presented with odd torsion) define a cellular automaton on $K^G$ that is injective but not surjective, so $G$ is not surjunctive. The odd-characteristic companion (September 26) gives the same conclusion over a field of order $p^4$ for a finitely generated group with torsion. The automata are linear; no torsion-free non-surjunctive group is claimed in these papers (the torsion-free companion does not discuss automata).
problems.aiRole: The release README says the results were produced by an unreleased internal OpenAI model with a fixed procedure, on average about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute per result, and that some outputs build on earlier model results. The cellular automaton is obtained from the direct-finiteness counterexample by the standard algebra-to-automaton transfer, proved in full in Section 6 of the principal manuscript.

problems.name: The periodic tiling conjecture in dimension three
problems.field: Translational tilings of lattices and Euclidean space
problems.statement: A finite nonempty $F\subset\mathbb Z^d$ is a translational tile if $A\oplus F=\mathbb Z^d$ for some $A$; the tiling is periodic if $A$ is invariant under a finite-index subgroup. The periodic tiling conjecture (Lagarias and Wang, 1996, also in a Euclidean form for bounded measurable tiles of $\mathbb R^d$) asserts that every translational tile admits a periodic tiling. It holds in $\mathbb Z$ (Newman) and $\mathbb Z^2$ (Bhattacharya), and Greenfeld and Tao disproved it in sufficiently high dimension. Does every finite translational tile of $\mathbb Z^3$, and every bounded tile of $\mathbb R^3$, admit a periodic tiling?
problems.posedBy: Jeffrey C. Lagarias and Yang Wang
problems.ageNote: Lagarias and Wang, Tiling the line with translates of one tile, Invent. Math. 124 (1996), p. 346, as cited by the manuscript. The dimension-three case became the open frontier after Greenfeld and Tao's high-dimensional counterexample (Annals 2024).
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: there is a finite nonempty $T\subset\mathbb Z^3$ that tiles $\mathbb Z^3$ by translations, but no translation set of a tiling is invariant under a finite-index subgroup; and $T+[0,1]^3$ tiles $\mathbb R^3$ up to null sets, with no tiling whose translation set is invariant under a full-rank lattice, even allowing real translations. With Bhattacharya's planar theorem, three is the least lattice dimension where periodic tiling fails. The tile is not claimed to be connected, and the result concerns full periodicity only, not the absence of every individual period.

problems.name: The purely cosmetic surgery conjecture for knots in the three-sphere
problems.field: Low-dimensional topology: Dehn surgery on knots
problems.statement: For a knot $K\subset S^3$ and a slope $r\in\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$, let $S^3_r(K)$ be the oriented manifold obtained by Dehn surgery. Two distinct slopes $r\ne s$ are purely cosmetic if $S^3_r(K)$ and $S^3_s(K)$ are orientation-preservingly homeomorphic. Gordon conjectured (as part of his cosmetic filling conjecture) that this never happens for a nontrivial knot; the question is Bleiler's Problem 1.81(A) in Kirby's list. Known before this work: the meridional case (Gordon-Luecke), same-sign pairs (Wu), the reduction to opposite slopes $\pm 2$ or $\pm 1/q$ (Ni-Wu, Hanselman), exclusion of $\pm 1/q$ (Daemi-Lidman-Miller Eismeier), and verification for many families and all knots up to about 19 crossings. Does every nontrivial knot $K\subset S^3$ satisfy: $S^3_r(K)\cong S^3_s(K)$ orientation-preservingly implies $r=s$?
problems.posedBy: C. McA. Gordon, Dehn surgery on knots, Proc. ICM Kyoto 1990 (published 1991), Conjecture 6.1; recorded as Bleiler's Problem 1.81(A) in Kirby's 1997 problem list
problems.ageNote: Gordon stated the conjecture in his 1990 ICM address, published in the proceedings in 1991 (the manuscript cites the 1991 volume). Kirby's 1997 list records it as Problem 1.81(A), attributed to Bleiler.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for every nontrivial smooth knot $K\subset S^3$ and all $r,s\in\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$, an orientation-preserving homeomorphism $S^3_r(K)\cong S^3_s(K)$ forces $r=s$; the homeomorphism need not preserve the surgery core or the knot exterior. After the cited reduction to $g(K)=2$ and slopes $\pm 2$, the paper derives a contradiction by comparing a nonzero integer instanton count $\Omega$ on a parameterized cobordism with a one-dimensional count of solutions with spinors whose boundary would force $2^\eta\Omega=0$. It does not address chirally cosmetic (orientation-reversing) surgeries or knots in other three-manifolds.

problems.name: The projective-space base conjecture for Lagrangian fibrations of compact hyperkahler manifolds
problems.shortName: Base of a Lagrangian fibration is P^n
problems.field: Complex and algebraic geometry; hyperkahler manifolds, Lagrangian fibrations
problems.statement: Let $f:X\to B$ be a fibration with connected fibres from a compact irreducible holomorphic symplectic Kahler manifold of dimension $2n$ onto a normal base with $0<\dim B<2n$. Matsushita showed $\dim B=n$ and the fibres are Lagrangian; Hwang proved $B\cong\mathbb P^n$ when $X$ is projective and $B$ is smooth, Greb-Lehn extended this to Kahler $X$, and the conclusion was known for the $K3^{[n]}$, Kummer, OG6 and OG10 types and in dimension four (Ou, Huybrechts-Xu). The projective-space base conjecture asks: is the normal base $B$ of such a fibration always isomorphic to $\mathbb P^n$, without assuming $B$ smooth?
problems.posedBy: Not named in the manuscript; it states the projective-space base conjecture in the setting of Matsushita (1999), Hwang (2008) and Greb-Lehn (2014)
problems.ageNote: The manuscript calls this the projective-space base conjecture but cites no poser or year; Hwang's 2008 smooth-base theorem is the earliest cited partial result. Left null rather than guessed.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: if $f:X\to B$ is a projective surjective connected-fibre morphism from a compact IHS Kahler manifold of dimension $2n$ onto a normal projective $n$-dimensional $B$, with every fibre component $n$-dimensional and isotropic for $\sigma$, then $B\cong\mathbb P^n$, with no smoothness assumption on $B$, no bound on $b_2$ and no restriction on deformation type. With Kim-Oguiso-Shinder it excludes codimension-one multiple fibres. Not shown: the case of a nonprojective $X$ (Kahler $X$ with a non-projective morphism).

problems.name: The Anari-Oveis Gharan-Vinzant perfect-matching entropy conjecture
problems.statement: Let $G$ be a graph on $n=2m$ vertices with $N(G)\ge1$ perfect matchings and perfect-matching polytope $P(G)$. For $x\in P(G)$ put $F(x)=-\sum_e x_e\log x_e$ and $B(x)=-\sum_e(1-x_e)\log(1-x_e)$. Anari, Oveis Gharan and Vinzant proposed a convex-programming approach to counting, in which $\max_{x\in P(G)}(F(x)+B(x))$ estimates $\log N(G)$; for bipartite graphs the Schrijver and Gurvits inequalities make it accurate. Is it true for every graph that $\max_{x\in P(G)}(F(x)+B(x))\le\log N(G)+O(n)$, that is, that the binary-coordinate entropy of a perfect-matching mean exceeds $\log N(G)$ by at most a linear function of the number of vertices?
problems.posedBy: Nima Anari, Shayan Oveis Gharan and Cynthia Vinzant, Log-concave polynomials, entropy, and a deterministic approximation algorithm for counting bases of matroids, FOCS 2018, Conjecture 6
problems.ageNote: Conjecture 6 of the FOCS 2018 version, as the manuscript cites it; the arXiv version (1807.00929) appeared in July 2018.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for a loopless multigraph on $2m\ge2$ vertices with a perfect matching and every $x\in P(G)$, boundary included, $F(x)-(2-2/m)B(x)\le H(x)\le F(x)$, where $H(x)$ is the maximum entropy of a law on perfect matchings with marginals $x$. Hence $\log N(G)\le\max_{x\in P(G)}(F+B)\le\log N(G)+3m-2$, the conjectured linear error with an explicit constant. Also proved: the sharp bound $|\mathrm{supp}\,x|-\dim F_x\le3m-2$ for the minimal face, and lower counts such as $N(G)\ge e^{-2(m-1)}k^m$ for $k$-regular graphs with all odd cuts of size at least $k$. The paper notes the bipartite coefficient-one inequality $H\ge F-B$ fails for a nonbipartite eight-vertex example.

problems.name: Almost-everywhere regularity of stationary integral varifolds
problems.field: Geometric measure theory: regularity of stationary varifolds
problems.statement: Let $V$ be a stationary integral $m$-varifold in an open set $U\subset\mathbb R^{m+n}$: an integer-multiplicity rectifiable $m$-dimensional measure whose first variation of area vanishes. A support point is regular if near it $V$ is a positive integer multiple of a single smooth embedded minimal submanifold. Allard (1972) proved that the regular set is relatively open and dense and that density-one points are regular, but at points with higher-multiplicity planar tangents his theorem does not apply. Simon's notes record the question, and Brena, Decio and De Lellis (2025, Conjecture 1.2) conjecture a positive answer. Is $\mathcal H^m(\mathrm{Sing}\,V)=0$ for every stationary integral $m$-varifold, in every dimension and codimension?
problems.posedBy: Leon Simon, Introduction to Geometric Measure Theory (notes, 2018), Ch. 5 Remark 6.4; stated as Conjecture 1.2 by Brena, Decio and De Lellis, Rend. Lincei Mat. Appl. 36 (2025)
problems.ageNote: 2018 is the earliest record the manuscript cites (Simon's revised notes); it gives Allard's 1972 theory as background but does not say the question was posed there, so no earlier year is given.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: every stationary integral $m$-varifold in an open subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$, $m,n\ge1$, has $\mathcal H^m(\mathrm{Sing}\,V)=0$, with no stability, minimizing, orientability, density-bound or codimension hypothesis. Corollary 1.2 gives the same on round spheres. The main new estimate is a signed excess bound in flat cylinders. The companion A Codimension-One Bound for the Singular Set of a Stationary Integral Varifold (5 Oct 2026) claims the stronger bound $\dim_{\mathcal H}\mathrm{Sing}\,V\le m-1$, which implies this one and is a separate entry; it uses this paper's signed-excess theorem as an input. Neither paper treats non-Euclidean ambient metrics, where De Lellis-Hirsch-Lihn-Spolaor construct exotic examples.

problems.name: The blockwise Alperin weight conjecture
problems.field: Modular representation theory of finite groups
problems.statement: Let $p$ be a prime and $G$ a finite group. A $p$-weight of $G$ is a pair $(Q,\phi)$ with $Q$ a $p$-subgroup and $\phi$ an irreducible character of $N_G(Q)/Q$ of $p$-defect zero; each weight is assigned to a $p$-block of $G$ by Brauer induction. For a block $B$, let $l(B)$ be the number of irreducible Brauer characters (simple modules) in $B$ and let $W_p(B)$ be the set of $G$-conjugacy classes of weights assigned to $B$. Alperin conjectured that simple modules are counted locally, block by block. Does $l(B)=|W_p(B)|$ hold for every prime $p$, every finite group $G$ and every $p$-block $B$?
problems.posedBy: J. L. Alperin, Weights for finite groups (Arcata conference 1986, proceedings 1987)
problems.ageNote: Formulated at the 1986 Arcata conference; the original account appeared in the 1987 proceedings, per the manuscript.
problems.resultNote: Claims $l(B)=|W_p(B)|$ for every prime $p$, finite group $G$ and $p$-block $B$, including the $Q=1$ case. Consequences derived: $l(B)\ge l(b)$ for the Brauer correspondent $b$, equality for abelian defect groups, the Sylow normalizer inequality for Brauer character counts, and principal-block bounds of Hung, Sambale and Tiep. The proof uses chain inversion and powers modulo commutators to reduce to counting tuples in groups with trivial $O_p$, then proves the needed $p$-power divisibility via moduli of marked genus-one covers. It is an equality of cardinalities only: no natural or equivariant bijection, and no inductive condition for simple groups, is established.
problems.aiRole: The release README says the manuscripts were produced by an unreleased internal OpenAI model, which was posed some 4,000 open research problems during an evaluation, with the vast majority of results obtained by one fixed procedure averaging about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute each. This manuscript is not among the README's named exceptions. It is credited to OpenAI with no human author named.
problems.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Theorem 1 was read against the posed conjecture and states the numerical blockwise form exactly, with no restriction on prime, group or defect group, using Brauer's central-character block induction. There is no Lean formalization for this manuscript in the release. Nothing was re-run here. A reader should know the proof route is unusual: it avoids the classification of finite simple groups and the inductive blockwise weight condition, reducing instead to a divisibility statement for tuple counts proved through high-index genus-one curve covers and inseparable genus change in characteristic p. The equivariant or canonical refinements of the conjecture are not claimed.
problems.significanceNote: One of the handful of central local-global conjectures of modular representation theory, open for almost forty years and the target of a long reduction program through finite simple groups; famous within algebra rather than across mathematics. Scored with the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture at 55, just below the Köthe Conjecture and Gromov and Weiss's Question on Sofic Groups at 60.

problems.name: Cardy's formula and conformal invariance for critical bond percolation on the square lattice
problems.shortName: Cardy's formula on the square lattice
problems.statement: Cardy (1992) predicted that for critical two-dimensional percolation the probability of an open crossing between two boundary arcs of a conformal quadrilateral converges to an explicit conformally invariant function, $\int_0^x[t(1-t)]^{-2/3}dt\,/\int_0^1[t(1-t)]^{-2/3}dt$ in the half-plane coordinate $x$. Smirnov (2001) proved it for site percolation on the triangular lattice, and Camia-Newman built the full loop limit there, but the proof uses the lattice's special symmetry. For the most standard model, bond percolation on $\mathbb Z^2$ at $p=1/2$, only partial or disputed claims existed. Does Cardy's formula, and conformal invariance of the exploration interface (convergence to $\mathrm{SLE}_6$), hold for critical bond percolation on the square lattice?
problems.posedBy: John Cardy, Critical percolation in finite geometries, J. Phys. A 25 (1992), as a physical prediction; the square-lattice case is the q = 1 case of Rohde-Schramm Conjecture 9.7 (2005)
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.2: for critical bond percolation on $\delta\mathbb Z^2$ in a Jordan domain with four uniformly approximated marks, all boundary edges sampled and no external connections, the probability of an open crossing between the arcs $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$ converges to Cardy's hypergeometric function of the cross-ratio. The $q=1$ case of Theorem 1.1 gives chordal $\mathrm{SLE}_6$ convergence of the exploration interface and CLE$_6$ convergence of all nested loops. The crossing result is proved directly, not from the curve limit. It does not treat other lattices or general boundary conditions beyond those stated.

problems.name: An FPRAS for counting common bases of two matroids
problems.shortName: Counting common bases of two matroids
problems.statement: Given independence oracles for two matroids $M_1,M_2$ of the same rank $r$ on $[n]$, estimate $|\mathcal B(M_1)\cap\mathcal B(M_2)|$, the number of common bases. The problem contains counting bases of one matroid (FPRAS by Anari-Liu-Oveis Gharan-Vinzant) and counting perfect matchings of a bipartite graph (the Jerrum-Sinclair-Vigoda permanent FPRAS). For intersections only coarse or exponential-factor approximations were known, and Anari-Oveis Gharan-Vinzant's $2^{O(r)}$-factor method is fully polynomial only for $r=O(\log n)$. Cryan, Guo and Mousa asked for a rapidly mixing chain sampling common bases. Is there a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for the number of common bases of two arbitrary matroids given by independence oracles?
problems.posedBy: Cryan, Guo and Mousa (Ann. Probab. 2021) asked for a fast sampler; the FPRAS question is Problem 1 of Section 13.2 of Kuikui Liu's dissertation (2023)
problems.ageNote: Year of the Cryan-Guo-Mousa journal version the manuscript cites; the question is likely older folklore in approximate counting, but the manuscript gives no earlier source.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: one randomized oracle algorithm, given independence oracles for rank-$r$ matroids on $[n]$ and rational $\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1)$, outputs $\widehat Z$ within relative error $\varepsilon$ of the number of common bases with probability at least $1-\delta$, outputs zero when there are none, and uses polynomially many oracle calls and bit operations on every execution. Corollaries give FPRASes and almost-uniform samplers for common independent sets of prescribed, unrestricted or maximum size, even for different ranks. The method is a Jerrum-Sinclair-Vigoda style annealed chain with defect states, using the homogeneous Tutte theorem of Branden-Huh (Lorentzian polynomials). It gives no exact counting and no deterministic algorithm, and does not treat three or more matroids. The October companion gives an FPRAS for common integer bases of two polymatroids with binary capacities.
problems.aiRole: The release README says the results were produced by an unreleased internal OpenAI model with one fixed procedure, on average about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute per result. This result is not among the README's exceptions (the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties and the Re(s) > 11/12 zero-free region, whose write-up was human-edited). The manuscript is authored 'OpenAI' and names no human author. A later manuscript in the family (5 October 2026) extends the method to common integer bases of two polymatroids with binary capacities and builds on this paper's transport and trace estimates.

problems.name: The coarse Novikov conjecture for bounded-geometry spaces: is coarse assembly rationally injective?
problems.field: Higher index theory; coarse geometry; operator K-theory
problems.statement: For a uniformly discrete metric space $X$ of bounded geometry, coarse K-homology $KX_*(X)=\varinjlim_r K_*^{lf}(P_r(X))$ is the limit over Rips complexes, and the coarse assembly map $\mu_X:KX_*(X)\to K_*(C^*(X))$ sends a class to its index in the K-theory of the Roe algebra. Roe formulated the coarse index theory and its Novikov-type injectivity question, and Higson and Roe (1995) stated the coarse Baum-Connes conjecture that $\mu_X$ is an isomorphism. Surjectivity was known to fail for some expanders (Higson-Lafforgue-Skandalis), while injectivity was proved under geometric hypotheses such as coarse embeddability in Hilbert space (Yu). The coarse Novikov conjecture asks: is $\mu_X\otimes\mathbb Q$ injective for every bounded-geometry space $X$?
problems.posedBy: John Roe, Coarse cohomology and index theory on complete Riemannian manifolds (Memoirs AMS 497, 1993); Nigel Higson and John Roe, On the coarse Baum-Connes conjecture (1995), Conjecture 6.6
problems.ageNote: The manuscripts credit Roe (1993) with the Novikov-type formulation and Higson-Roe (1995, Conjecture 6.6) with the coarse Baum-Connes conjecture, of which rational injectivity is the Novikov half; no single posing sentence for the bounded-geometry injectivity statement is quoted.
problems.resultNote: Claims a uniformly discrete bounded-geometry space $X$, a coarse disjoint union of finite connected graphs of uniformly bounded degree, with an infinite-order class $\alpha\in KX_1(X)$ whose image under ordinary coarse assembly into $K_1$ of the reduced locally compact Roe algebra vanishes, so $\mu_X$ fails to be injective integrally and rationally. The companion (5 October 2026) claims the same kind of class is killed already by maximal coarse assembly, which implies the reduced statement. Earlier kernel examples (Yu; Dranishnikov-Ferry-Weinberger) lacked bounded geometry or died under coarsening. It does NOT give a counterexample to the Novikov conjecture or to Baum-Connes for groups, nor a space with property A or coarsely embeddable into Hilbert space.
problems.aiRole: The release README says all results were produced by an unreleased internal OpenAI model, the vast majority by one fixed procedure using on average about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute per result. Its named exceptions (the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties, and the Re(s) > 11/12 zero-free region, whose write-up was human edited for readability) do not concern this family. Both manuscripts are credited to OpenAI with no human author named. The family has two manuscripts: the reduced counterexample (23 September 2026), taken as principal here, and a 5 October 2026 strengthening to maximal Roe algebras. The reduced result has a Lean comparator challenge in the release.
problems.verificationNote: No independent mathematician has checked this yet. Theorem 1.1 of both manuscripts was read against the coarse Novikov conjecture. problems.name: Long-time nonequilibrium fluctuations of the hard-sphere gas (finite-dimensional laws)
problems.statement: Beyond the Boltzmann equation, the fluctuations of the empirical measure of a dilute hard-sphere gas are expected to be Gaussian and governed by the linear fluctuating Boltzmann equation. Bodineau, Gallagher, Saint-Raymond and Simonella proved this for short times away from equilibrium and for long times at equilibrium. After deriving the Boltzmann equation on every regular kinetic interval, Deng, Hani and Ma identified long-time nonequilibrium fluctuations as a further application of their method. Do the fluctuations of a hard-sphere gas converge to the Gaussian solution of the linear fluctuating Boltzmann equation throughout every interval on which the Boltzmann solution is regular, without an equilibrium or small-data assumption?
problems.posedBy: Yu Deng, Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma (arXiv 2408.07818, Section 1.4.3)
problems.ageNote: The manuscript cites the 2025 version of the Deng-Hani-Ma preprint, first posted in 2024.
problems.resultNote: For a deterministic grand-canonical hard-sphere gas in $\mathbb R^3$ with smooth initial density having summable Gaussian bounds on it and its gradient, on every $[0,T]$ where the Boltzmann solution has uniform Gaussian velocity decay, the empirical measure centered at its exact microscopic expectation and scaled by $\sqrt{\mu_\varepsilon}$ has finite-dimensional distributions converging to those of the Gaussian solution of the linear fluctuating Boltzmann equation. It does not prove process-level convergence or tightness, does not treat periodic domains (the BGSS setting) or potentials, and assumes the regular kinetic solution exists.

problems.name: The Rohde-Schramm conjecture: critical square-lattice FK interfaces converge to SLE for 1 <= q < 4 (and 0 < q < 1 in smooth domains)
problems.field: Statistical mechanics; random-cluster model, SLE and CLE scaling limits
problems.statement: In the random-cluster (FK) model on the square lattice with cluster weight $q$ at the self-dual point $p_q=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$, the Dobrushin interface in a domain with two marked boundary points is expected to have a conformally invariant scaling limit. Rohde and Schramm (2005, Conjecture 9.7), restated by Schramm (ICM 2006, Problem 2.6), conjectured for every fixed $0<q<4$ that it converges to chordal $\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa}$ with $\kappa=4\pi/\arccos(-\sqrt q/2)$. Before this work it was proved only for $q=2$ (FK-Ising, Smirnov and Chelkak-Smirnov) and, for site percolation on the triangular lattice, the analogous $q=1$ statement. Does the critical square-lattice FK interface converge to $\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa(q)}$ for every $0<q<4$?
problems.posedBy: Steffen Rohde and Oded Schramm, Basic properties of SLE, Ann. of Math. 161 (2005), Conjecture 9.7; Schramm, ICM 2006 (2007), Problem 2.6
problems.resultNote: For every fixed $1\le q<4$ (September 23), and $1\le q\le4$ (October 5 companion), critical square-lattice FK Dobrushin interfaces converge to chordal $\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa(q)}$ in every bounded Jordan domain with uniformly approximated marks, and the complete nested loop collection of the free infinite-volume measure converges to whole-plane $\mathrm{CLE}_{\kappa(q)}$, keeping multiplicities and traversals. problems.name: Dixmier's unitarizability problem for discrete groups
problems.field: Group theory; amenability and uniformly bounded representations
problems.statement: A representation $\pi:G\to GL(H)$ of a discrete group on a Hilbert space is uniformly bounded if $\sup_g\|\pi(g)\|<\infty$, and unitarizable if some bounded invertible $S$ makes every $S\pi(g)S^{-1}$ unitary; $G$ is unitarizable if every uniformly bounded representation is. Day and Dixmier (1950) showed amenable groups are unitarizable, and groups containing a nonabelian free subgroup are not (Ehrenpreis-Mautner, Pytlik-Szwarc). Partial converses were known via Pisier's quantitative criterion, Epstein-Monod, Osin, Monod-Ozawa and Vergara. Dixmier asked whether unitarizability characterizes amenability: is every unitarizable discrete group amenable?
problems.posedBy: Jacques Dixmier, Les moyennes invariantes dans les semi-groupes et leurs applications, Acta Sci. Math. (Szeged) 12 (1950), section 5, p. 221
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: a discrete group is amenable if and only if every uniformly bounded representation on every complex Hilbert space is similar to a unitary one. For every nonamenable $G$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a representation with $\sup_g\|\pi(g)\|\le1+\varepsilon$ not similar to a unitary one, on a separable space if $G$ is countable. This settles Dixmier's question for all discrete groups. Not shown: anything for nondiscrete locally compact groups, or a bound on similarity degree beyond what the theorem gives.

problems.name: The Morse-number Arnold conjecture for nondegenerate Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms
problems.field: Symplectic topology; Hamiltonian fixed points, Morse theory
problems.statement: For a closed connected symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$ let $\mathrm{Morse}(M)$ be the least number of critical points of a Morse function on $M$. Floer theory and its virtual extensions show that a nondegenerate Hamiltonian diffeomorphism has at least the sum of the Betti numbers many fixed points, but the Morse number can be larger. The Morse-number form of the Arnold conjecture asks: if $H$ is a one-periodic Hamiltonian whose time-one map is nondegenerate, is the number of fixed points with contractible orbits at least $\mathrm{Morse}(M)$?
problems.posedBy: V. I. Arnold, First steps in symplectic topology (1986); recorded as Conjecture 1.1 in R. Golovko, On variants of Arnold conjecture, Arch. Math. (Brno) 56 (2020)
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: there are a closed symplectic 12-manifold and a one-periodic Hamiltonian with all fixed points nondegenerate and contractible and $\#\mathrm{Fix}=\chi(M)+128<\mathrm{Morse}(M)$; Corollary 1.2 makes $\mathrm{Morse}(M)-\#\mathrm{Fix}$ arbitrarily large (the manifold depends on the deficit). The mechanism: the augmentation ideal of $A_5^k$ needs two generators while $d(A_5^k)$ is unbounded, realized by relative handle cancellation on $X\times\mathbb R^8$. The fixed-point count still exceeds the homological (Floer) bounds. The examples are not simply connected; the October 5 companions give simply connected Kahler examples below the stable Morse number.
problems.claimIssueNote: The release says: 'Ma [Theorem 1.5] asserted that the minimum number of fixed points over all Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms always equals Crit(M). Theorem 1.1 contradicts that assertion' (degenerate paper) and 'Ma's preprint asserts that the minimum number of fixed points of a nondegenerate Hamiltonian diffeomorphism always equals the ordinary Morse number ... Theorem 1.1 contradicts that unrestricted assertion' (Morse-number paper). The other side: R. Ma, Proofs on Arnold conjectures, arXiv 0808.0613v7 (2013), Theorem 1.5, claims these lower bounds hold in general. Ma's preprint is unpublished; no referee has ruled between them.

problems.name: Turyn's conjecture that binary merit factors are bounded
problems.statement: For a binary word $A=(a_0,\dots,a_{N-1})\in\{-1,1\}^N$ with aperiodic autocorrelations $C_u(A)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1-u}a_ja_{j+u}$, the merit factor is $F(A)=N^2/(2\sum_{u=1}^{N-1}C_u(A)^2)$. Equivalently $1/F(A)=\|P_A\|_4^4/N^2-1$ for the polynomial $P_A(z)=\sum a_jz^j$ on the unit circle. The best proven constructions, from modified Legendre sequences, reach limiting merit factor about $6.34$ (Jedwab, Katz and Schmidt). Turyn's conjecture, equivalently Erdos's $L^4$-norm conjecture, asserts that $F(A)$ is bounded over all binary words of all lengths. Is the merit factor of binary sequences bounded?
problems.posedBy: Richard J. Turyn (name as used by Downarowicz and Lacroix 1998); equivalently Erdos's L4-norm conjecture
problems.ageNote: The manuscript cites Downarowicz and Lacroix (Theoret. Comput. Sci. 1998), who call the boundedness conjecture Turyn's conjecture, equivalently Erdos's L4-norm conjecture. Neither the manuscript nor that citation as quoted gives the year Turyn stated it, so the year is left blank.
problems.resultNote: Section 8 deduces from Theorem 1.1 (real-sign polynomials of every large length with maximum $(1+o(1))\sqrt N$) that $\max_{A\in\{-1,1\}^N}F(A)\to\infty$ as $N\to\infty$ through all integers, disproving Turyn's conjecture in this all-length form. Via Downarowicz and Lacroix it also gives a uniquely ergodic binary Morse shift with simple spectrum and absolutely continuous zero-coordinate spectral measure with $L^2$ density. The construction is existential: no explicit sequences, no rate and no algorithm are given.

problems.name: The Boone-Higman conjecture: groups with solvable word problem embed in finitely presented simple groups
problems.field: Combinatorial group theory; word problem and embedding theorems
problems.statement: Higman's embedding theorem (1961) characterizes finitely generated subgroups of finitely presented groups as the recursively presented groups. Boone and Higman (1974) proved that a finitely generated group has solvable word problem if and only if it embeds in a simple group that in turn embeds in a finitely presented group, and asked whether the simple overgroup itself can be chosen finitely presented. Thompson later obtained a finitely generated simple overgroup, and the conjecture was proved for hyperbolic groups, Baumslag-Solitar and free-by-cyclic groups, $\mathrm{Out}(F_n)$ and mapping class groups, among others. Does every finitely generated group with solvable word problem embed in a finitely presented simple group?
problems.posedBy: William W. Boone and Graham Higman (J. Austral. Math. Soc. 18, 1974, p. 43)
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: a finitely generated group has decidable word problem if and only if it embeds in a finitely presented simple group. The route is Theorem 1.2: every such group embeds in a finitely presented group with a faithful two-transitive action on a countable set with finitely generated point stabilizers, built as a mapping torus of an affine Steinberg group over finitely presented $\mathbb F_2$-algebras, which Zaremsky's criterion for twisted Brin-Thompson groups turns into a finitely presented simple overgroup. The higher-finiteness strengthening is the companion's separate entry; no explicit bound on the size of the presentation is given.

problems.name: Nagata's conjecture on plane curves through very general points
problems.field: Algebraic geometry; linear systems of plane curves
problems.statement: Let $p_1,\dots,p_r$ be very general points of the complex projective plane. Nagata, in his work on Hilbert's fourteenth problem, conjectured that for $r\ge 10$ every nonzero effective plane curve $C$ of degree $d$ with $\mathrm{mult}_{p_i}C\ge m_i$ satisfies $\sum_{i=1}^r m_i < d\sqrt r$. He proved it when $r$ is a perfect square at least $16$. The bound fails at $r=9$ (a cubic through nine points), and partial results (Roé, Harbourne, Ciliberto-Miranda degenerations, the $117/37$ bound at ten points) left every nonsquare $r\ge10$ open. Equivalently, the multipoint Seshadri constant of a line at $r\ge10$ very general points is $1/\sqrt r$. Does the strict inequality $\sum_i m_i<d\sqrt r$ hold for every $r\ge 10$, every degree and every multiplicity vector?
problems.posedBy: Masayoshi Nagata
problems.ageNote: Nagata, On the 14-th problem of Hilbert, Amer. J. Math. 81 (1959), cited by the manuscript; see also his Tata lectures (1965).
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for every $r\ge10$ there is a countable union $E_r$ of proper Zariski-closed subsets of the configuration space, with nonempty complement, such that for every $(p_1,\dots,p_r)\notin E_r$, every nonzero effective plane curve $C$ of degree $d\ge1$ and all $m_i\le\mathrm{mult}_{p_i}C$, one has $\sum m_i<d\sqrt r$. Reducible and nonreduced curves and unequal multiplicities are included. Section 6 deduces that the multipoint Seshadri constant of a line is $1/\sqrt r$ and extends the theorem to every uncountable algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. It does not treat positive characteristic in this manuscript, and it does not address the SHGH conjecture or other finer statements about linear systems.

problems.name: Kirchberg's embedding problem: does every separable C*-algebra embed in a norm ultrapower of the Cuntz algebra O2?
problems.field: Operator algebras; model theory of C*-algebras
problems.statement: Kirchberg and Phillips proved that every separable unital exact C*-algebra embeds unitally into the Cuntz algebra $\mathcal O_2$. Kirchberg asked how far this universality extends beyond exact algebras once $\mathcal O_2$ is replaced by its norm ultrapower $\mathcal O_2^\omega$. Goldbring and Sinclair (2015) named this Kirchberg's embedding problem and showed its equivalence with existential closedness statements; it is distinct from Connes' embedding problem and from the tensor-norm form of Kirchberg's QWEP conjecture. Does every separable unital C*-algebra admit a unital embedding into $\mathcal O_2^\omega$ for a free ultrafilter $\omega$ on $\mathbb N$?
problems.posedBy: Eberhard Kirchberg, as recorded and named by Isaac Goldbring and Thomas Sinclair, On Kirchberg's embedding problem (J. Funct. Anal., 2015)
problems.ageNote: Year of the first citable statement, Goldbring-Sinclair 2015, which recounts that Kirchberg considered the question after the Kirchberg-Phillips embedding theorem (2000); when Kirchberg first raised it is not dated there.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for $G=\mathbb Z[1/2]^3\rtimes(\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbb Z)\times\mathbb Z)$ with $(M,k)\cdot v=2^kMv$, the full group C*-algebra $C^*(G)$ is separable and unital and has no unital embedding into $B^\omega$ for any nonzero unital nuclear $B$ and any free ultrafilter $\omega$; in particular none into $\mathcal O_2^\omega$. The obstruction combines property (T) of $\mathbb Z^3\rtimes\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbb Z)$ with a finiteness lemma for approximate representation types in nuclear algebras. Via Goldbring-Sinclair it follows that no exact or nuclear unital C*-algebra is existentially closed. It says nothing about Connes' embedding problem or the QWEP conjecture.

problems.name: Explicit nonbipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree
problems.statement: A $d$-regular graph is Ramanujan if every nonconstant adjacency eigenvalue $\lambda$ satisfies $|\lambda|\le2\sqrt{d-1}$, the Alon-Boppana optimum. Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak and Margulis built explicit Ramanujan families only for $d=p+1$, Morgenstern extended this to $d=q+1$ for prime powers $q$, and Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava proved existence of bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree. Existence of nonbipartite ones in every degree now follows from random-graph universality (Huang, McKenzie, Yau), but non-constructively. For every fixed $d\ge3$, can nonbipartite $d$-regular Ramanujan graphs be constructed deterministically, in polynomial time, at every large size?
problems.posedBy: Alexander Lubotzky, Ralph Phillips and Peter Sarnak
problems.ageNote: The manuscript cites Lubotzky-Phillips-Sarnak (1988) and Morgenstern (1994); Morgenstern's abstract describes his construction as a partial solution to a problem raised by Lubotzky, Phillips and Sarnak. The manuscript itself does not quote a posing sentence.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for every $d\ge3$ there are $n_0(d)$, $k_d$ and a deterministic algorithm that, on every even $n\ge n_0(d)$, outputs the adjacency list of a simple connected nonbipartite $d$-regular graph on $n$ vertices whose nonconstant eigenvalues lie strictly between $\pm2\sqrt{d-1}$, in $O_d(n^{k_d})$ bit operations. The construction uses partial pairings, deterministic resolvent estimates, cleanup and an exact spectral repair step. It is not strongly explicit (no local adjacency queries), and the exponent may grow with $d$.

problems.name: Schafhauser-Tikuisis-White Problem XXI: tracial real rank zero implies uniform property Gamma
problems.statement: Let $A$ be a unital separable simple infinite-dimensional nuclear stably finite C*-algebra with traces, $B$ its uniform tracial completion, and $B^\omega$ the uniform tracial ultrapower along a free ultrafilter. Uniform property $\Gamma$ asks for central projections that halve every limit trace on every coefficient. Schafhauser, Tikuisis and White asked (Problem XXI, in their completion-and-halving formulation) whether real rank zero of $B^\omega$ forces uniform property $\Gamma$. Does real rank zero of the uniform tracial ultrapower imply uniform property $\Gamma$?
problems.posedBy: Christopher Schafhauser, Aaron Tikuisis and Stuart White
problems.ageNote: Schafhauser, Tikuisis and White, Nuclear C*-algebras: 99 problems (arXiv 2506.10902, 2025), Section 6, Problem XXI, Definition 16.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for $A$ unital, separable, simple, infinite-dimensional, nuclear and stably finite with $T(A)\neq\emptyset$, if $B^\omega$ has real rank zero then there is a projection $p\in B^\omega\cap B'$ with $\lambda(px)=\lambda(x)/2$ for all $x\in B$ and all limit traces $\lambda$, so $A$ has uniform property $\Gamma$; it also identifies all traces on $B$. It does not show that real rank zero of $B^\omega$ holds in general, and Toms (2026) has shown nuclearity alone does not give uniform property $\Gamma$.

problems.name: Kobayashi's conjecture: a compact Kahler manifold with no entire curves has ample canonical bundle
problems.statement: A compact complex manifold $X$ is Kobayashi hyperbolic exactly when every holomorphic map $\mathbb C\to X$ is constant (Brody). Kobayashi conjectured that hyperbolicity forces positivity of the canonical bundle: a compact Kahler hyperbolic manifold should have ample $K_X$, and hence be projective. Known results needed metric hypotheses: negative or quasi-negative holomorphic sectional curvature (Wu-Yau, Tosatti-Yang, Diverio-Trapani), or Kahler hyperbolicity in Gromov's sense (Chen-Yang); without rational curves $K_X$ is known to be nef (Ou, Cao-Horing), but bigness was open. Is $K_X$ ample for every compact Kahler manifold of positive dimension that contains no nonconstant entire curve?
problems.posedBy: Shoshichi Kobayashi
problems.ageNote: Kobayashi, Hyperbolic Manifolds and Holomorphic Mappings (Marcel Dekker, 1970), cited by the manuscript as the source of the theory; Diverio's 2020 survey discusses the conjecture.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: if $X$ is a compact connected Kahler manifold of positive dimension and every holomorphic map $\mathbb C\to X$ is constant, then $K_X$ is ample and $X$ is projective. Corollaries: $K_X^{\otimes m}$ is globally generated for $m\ge n+2$ (using the release's Fujita freeness result), and a finite cover splits as a ball-quotient-type factor times a hyperbolic factor when the universal cover is semialgebraic. It does not cover singular spaces, non-Kahler compact complex manifolds, or the converse direction (Green-Griffiths-Lang type statements).

The family is a single manuscript (September 23, 2026). Its two corollaries cite other results from the same release (Fujita freeness and a semialgebraic-cover classification); the main theorem does not use them.

problems.name: Kadison's Similarity Problem
problems.statement: Kadison (1955) asked whether every bounded unital homomorphism $\pi$ from a unital $C^*$-algebra $A$ into the bounded operators $B(H)$ on a Hilbert space is similar to a $*$-homomorphism, that is, whether there is a bounded invertible $S$ such that $S\pi(\cdot)S^{-1}$ is a $*$-homomorphism. Known cases included nuclear algebras (Bunce, Christensen), cyclic representations and algebras without tracial states (Haagerup) and II$_1$ factors with property $\Gamma$ (Christensen). Haagerup showed similarity is equivalent to complete boundedness, and Kirchberg showed the problem is equivalent to the derivation problem. Is every bounded representation of a $C^*$-algebra on Hilbert space similar to a $*$-representation?
problems.posedBy: Richard V. Kadison, On the orthogonalization of operator representations, Amer. J. Math. 77 (1955)
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for every unital $C^*$-algebra $A$, every complex Hilbert space $H$ and every bounded complex-linear unital homomorphism $\pi:A\to B(H)$ there is a bounded invertible $S$ with $S\pi(\cdot)S^{-1}$ a $*$-homomorphism. It goes through Theorem 1.2, an absolute-constant commutator bound $\|[Y^{(h)},X]\|\le C\,g_P(Y)\|X\|$ over all von Neumann algebras $P$, all $Y$ and all matrix amplifications, combined with Kirchberg's derivation criterion. Corollary 1.3: every von Neumann algebra is hyperreflexive with constant at most $2C$, a statement known to be equivalent to a positive answer (Eleftherakis-Paulsen). No bound on the condition number of $S$ and no value of $C$ is given.

problems.name: The Mezard-Parisi formula for diluted spin glasses: the Panchenko-Talagrand equality conjecture
problems.field: Spin glass theory; diluted mean-field models
problems.statement: In diluted spin glasses such as the Viana-Bray model each spin has a finite mean number of interactions. Mezard and Parisi proposed a hierarchical cavity description of the limiting free energy by nested laws of local fields, with replica symmetry breaking. Franz-Leone obtained replica-symmetric and one-step bounds for even arity by Guerra's interpolation, and Panchenko and Talagrand proved the arbitrary finite-level hierarchical upper bounds for Poisson even-arity Ising models with factorized interactions under a positivity condition, conjecturing equality. In that class, is the limiting pressure equal to the infimum of the Mezard-Parisi trial functional over all finite hierarchy depths and trial laws?
problems.posedBy: Dmitry Panchenko and Michel Talagrand, 'Bounds for diluted mean-fields spin glass models' (PTRF 2004), conjecture after Theorem 4
problems.ageNote: The physical prediction is Mezard-Parisi (2001); the precise variational equality conjecture proved here is the one stated by Panchenko-Talagrand in 2004.
problems.resultNote: Main theorem: for Poisson-diluted even-arity Ising models in the Panchenko-Talagrand class (factorized interactions $e^{\theta}=a(1+b\prod f_l)$ with the stated independence and positivity of moments of $-b$), with only first moments of the interaction and field, the limiting pressure exists and equals $\inf_r$ of the infimum of the Mezard-Parisi hierarchical functional of depth $r$. Covers Viana-Bray, symmetric diluted even-spin models and soft random even-$K$ SAT at positive temperature. Not covered: odd arity (for example K-SAT with odd K), models outside the positivity class, fixed-degree random regular graphs, identification of the optimal hierarchy depth, or zero temperature beyond the stated ground-state limits.

problems.name: The one-dimensional Lieb-Thirring conjecture for $1/2<\gamma<3/2$
problems.statement: For $0\le W\in L^{\gamma+1/2}(\mathbb R)$ the Lieb-Thirring inequality reads $\sum_j|\lambda_j(-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}-W)|^\gamma\le L_{\gamma,1}\int_{\mathbb R}W^{\gamma+1/2}$. The sharp constant is the semiclassical one for $\gamma\ge3/2$ (Lieb-Thirring, Aizenman-Lieb) and equals $1/2$ at $\gamma=1/2$ (Hundertmark-Lieb-Thomas). For $1/2<\gamma<3/2$, Lieb and Thirring conjectured that the optimal constant equals the one-bound-state constant $L^{(1)}_{\gamma,1}$, the best constant when only the lowest eigenvalue is counted. Is $L_{\gamma,1}=L^{(1)}_{\gamma,1}$ for every $1/2<\gamma<3/2$?
problems.posedBy: Elliott H. Lieb and Walter E. Thirring (1976)
problems.ageNote: Conjecture from Lieb-Thirring, 'Inequalities for the moments of the eigenvalues of the Schrodinger Hamiltonian and their relation to Sobolev inequalities' (Bargmann Festschrift, 1976). The case gamma = 1 was proved by Read and Schulz (2026) before this work; the paper claims the remaining cases.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for every $1/2<\gamma<3/2$ and $0\le W\in L^{\gamma+1/2}(\mathbb R)$, $\mathrm{Tr}(H_{-W})_-^\gamma\le2(\frac{\gamma-1/2}{\gamma+1/2})^{\gamma-1/2}L^{cl}_{\gamma,1}\int W^{\gamma+1/2}$; the constant equals $L^{(1)}_{\gamma,1}$ and is attained by $(r+1)\mathrm{sech}^2(rx)$, $r=(\gamma-1/2)^{-1}$. Companions extend the same constant to Hermitian matrix potentials of any finite size (noncommuting, any rank) and classify all equality cases as direct sums of scalar solitons and zero channels. The scalar paper does not classify optimizers, and nothing is claimed in dimensions above one.

problems.name: Calderon's uniqueness question for bounded measurable scalar conductivities in dimension three
problems.statement: Calderon (1980) posed the inverse conductivity problem for real scalar conductivities $\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0<c\le\gamma\le C$: does the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma$ determine $\gamma$? In the plane Astala and Paivarinta (2006) proved uniqueness for all bounded measurable conductivities. In dimension $n\ge3$ uniqueness was proved under derivative regularity only: smooth (Sylvester-Uhlmann), Lipschitz (Caro-Rogers), $W^{1,n}$ in dimensions three and four (Haberman). Does $\Lambda_\gamma$ determine a bounded measurable, uniformly positive scalar conductivity in dimension $n\ge3$?
problems.posedBy: Alberto P. Calderon, On an inverse boundary value problem (1980)
problems.ageNote: Calderon posed the problem for bounded measurable conductivities in all dimensions; the plane was settled in 2006, leaving dimension at least three open, as the manuscript describes.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: there are real $\gamma_0,\gamma_1\in L^\infty(B(0,3))$ with $c\le\gamma_j\le C$, both equal to 1 near the boundary, differing on a set of positive measure, whose full weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann operators $H^{1/2}\to H^{-1/2}$ coincide. A corollary places $2^m$ such conductivities in any bounded Lipschitz domain in $\mathbb R^3$. The construction nests scalar blocks with toroidal interfaces. This refutes the uniqueness assertion quantified over all $n\ge3$. Not shown: counterexamples in each dimension $n\ge4$, control of the contrast, or anything about conductivities with some derivative regularity (where uniqueness is known).

The manuscripts are authored 'OpenAI' and name no human author. This entry rests on one manuscript dated September 23, 2026; the family's two smooth-uniqueness manuscripts are a separate entry.

problems.name: The Harary-Hill conjecture on the crossing number of complete graphs
problems.statement: The crossing number $\mathrm{cr}(G)$ is the least number of crossing points in a drawing of $G$ in the plane, with vertices at distinct points and edges as simple arcs meeting in finitely many proper crossings. Hill's construction (with earlier upper bounds by Guy, 1960) draws $K_n$ with $Z(n)=\frac14\lfloor\frac n2\rfloor\lfloor\frac{n-1}2\rfloor\lfloor\frac{n-2}2\rfloor\lfloor\frac{n-3}2\rfloor$ crossings, and Harary and Hill (1963) conjectured that this is optimal. It was verified only for $n\le12$ (and reported for $n\le14$), for restricted drawing classes, and asymptotically up to a factor of about $0.986$. Is $\mathrm{cr}(K_n)=Z(n)$ for every $n$?
problems.posedBy: Frank Harary and Anthony Hill, On the number of crossings in a complete graph (Proc. Edinburgh Math. Soc., 1963); upper bound earlier in Guy (1960)
problems.ageNote: The manuscript cites Harary-Hill (1963) for the conjecture and Guy's 1960 note for the first published upper bound; the conjecture is also often called Guy's conjecture.
problems.resultNote: Claims $\mathrm{cr}(K_n)=\frac14\lfloor\frac n2\rfloor\lfloor\frac{n-1}2\rfloor\lfloor\frac{n-2}2\rfloor\lfloor\frac{n-3}2\rfloor$ for every $n$, by a lower bound from signed intersections of cycles and an even-node order detector, plus a matching two-page drawing. Crossings are counted as points, every repeated crossing of an edge pair included. It does NOT address the rectilinear crossing number, the pair crossing number or the odd crossing number, which are different parameters.
problems.aiRole: The release README says the manuscripts were produced by an unreleased internal OpenAI model, the vast majority by one fixed procedure using on average about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute per result, and that some outputs build on earlier results produced by the models. Its named exceptions to that procedure (the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties and the zeta zero-free region work) do not concern this family. The manuscript is credited to OpenAI with no human author named.

Theorem 1.1 was read against the posed problem: $\mathrm{cr}(K_n)=Z(n)$ for all $n\ge3$ under the ordinary point-count convention, with unrestricted vertex positions and edge routes. formalization.yaml lists OAI.Paper170.complete_graph_crossing_number (comparator CompleteCrossing) as the main result. problems.name: The forcing conjecture for bipartite graphs
problems.statement: A graph $F$ with $m$ edges is $p$-forcing if every sequence of graphs $G_n$ with edge density tending to $p$ and $t(F,G_n)\to p^m$ is quasirandom of density $p$, and forcing if this holds for every $p\in(0,1)$. Chung, Graham and Wilson showed the four-cycle is forcing; Skokan and Thoma asked which bipartite graphs can replace it. Conlon, Fox and Sudakov formulated the forcing conjecture: a graph is forcing if and only if it is bipartite and contains a cycle. The conjecture implies Sidorenko's conjecture. Is every bipartite graph containing a cycle forcing?
problems.posedBy: Question of J. Skokan and L. Thoma (Graphs Combin., 2004); conjecture formulated by D. Conlon, J. Fox and B. Sudakov (GAFA, 2010, Conjecture 2)
problems.ageNote: Dated to Skokan and Thoma's 2004 question as the manuscript describes it; the precise conjecture is stated in Conlon, Fox and Sudakov (2010).
problems.resultNote: Corollary 1.3: for the same connected bipartite $H$ (which contains cycles) there are $p\in(0,1)$ and a nonconstant graphon $W$ with $t(K_2,W)=p$ and $t(H,W)=p^{66}$; sampling gives finite graphs with edge and $H$-densities tending to $p$ and $p^{66}$ but four-cycle density tending to a limit above $p^4$. So $H$ is not $p$-forcing at that $p$, and the conjecture fails. Since the forcing conjecture implies Sidorenko's, this follows from the Sidorenko counterexample; no separate idea is claimed.

problems.name: Donaldson's hypersymplectic deformation conjecture: deforming hypersymplectic four-manifolds to hyperkahler triples in fixed cohomology
problems.field: Differential geometry: hypersymplectic and hyperkahler four-manifolds
problems.statement: A hypersymplectic structure on a closed oriented four-manifold $X$ is a triple $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)$ of closed two-forms whose pointwise span is three-dimensional and positive definite for the wedge product. Donaldson (2006, Section 5.3, Question 3) asked whether a compact oriented four-manifold carrying such a triple admits a hyperkahler structure, and proposed a continuity method keeping the cohomology classes fixed. Fine and Yao formulated the normalized deformation problem as a conjecture: after normalizing $\int_X\omega_i\wedge\omega_j=\delta_{ij}$, can every hypersymplectic triple be deformed through hypersymplectic triples, keeping each class $[\omega_i]$ fixed, to a hyperkahler triple, i.e. one with $\omega_i\wedge\omega_j=2\delta_{ij}\mu$ for a volume form $\mu$? Known before this work: convergence of the hypersymplectic flow for simple-type structures on $T^4$ (Huang-Wang-Yao), $T^3$-invariant triples on $T^4$ (Fine-He-Yao) and triples preserved by a circle action. Does every normalized hypersymplectic triple on a closed four-manifold deform, with its cohomology classes fixed, to a hyperkahler triple?
problems.posedBy: S. K. Donaldson, Two-forms on four-manifolds and elliptic equations (2006), Section 5.3, Question 3; deformation form stated as Conjecture 1.1 by J. Fine and C. Yao (Duke Math. J. 2018)
problems.ageNote: Donaldson's question appeared in the 2006 Chern memorial volume (arXiv math/0607083). The cohomology-preserving deformation statement is Fine and Yao's Conjecture 1.1 (arXiv 1704.07620, 2017; Duke Math. J. 167, 2018).
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for a closed connected oriented smooth four-manifold $X$ and a smooth hypersymplectic triple with $\int_X\omega_i\wedge\omega_j=\delta_{ij}$, there is a smooth path $\omega(t)$ of hypersymplectic triples with $\omega(0)=\omega$, $[\omega_i(t)]=[\omega_i]$, ending at forms with $\omega_i(1)\wedge\omega_j(1)=2\delta_{ij}\mu_1$, parallel and self-dual for a hyperkahler metric. An arbitrary positive triple is reduced to this case by a constant linear change. Corollaries: every nonzero combination $\sum c_i\omega_i$ is Kahler for some hyperkahler metric, and any closed four-manifold with a positive closed triple is diffeomorphic to the K3 manifold or $T^4$. problems.name: Kurosh's problem for division rings: are algebraic division rings locally finite?
problems.statement: A division ring $D$ with center $F$ is algebraic over $F$ if every element satisfies a nonzero polynomial over $F$, and locally finite if every finite subset generates a division subring of finite dimension over $F$. In 1941, in connection with Burnside's problem, Kurosh asked whether a division ring that is algebraic and finitely generated as an algebra over a central subfield must be finite-dimensional over it. Golod's nil algebras answer the analogous question for general algebras but contain nilpotents, so they do not touch division rings; Jacobson and Kaplansky settled the bounded-degree and polynomial-identity cases. Is every division ring that is algebraic over its center locally finite?
problems.posedBy: A. G. Kurosh, Ringtheoretische Probleme, die mit dem Burnsideschen Problem uber periodische Gruppen in Zusammenhang stehen (1941), Problem (K)
problems.resultNote: Claims Theorem 1.1: there is a countable division ring $D$ of characteristic zero with center $F$ and $x,y\in D$ such that $D=F[x,y]=F(x,y)$, $[D:F]=\infty$, and every element of $D$ is algebraic over $F$ (with no uniform degree bound). So algebraicity over the center does not imply local finiteness. It does NOT give an example in positive characteristic or over a prescribed center, and polynomial degrees grow without bound, as they must by Jacobson's theorem.

problems.name: Erdos Problem #138: do the van der Waerden numbers grow superexponentially, W(k)^(1/k) -> infinity?
problems.statement: Let $W(k)$ be the least $N$ such that every two-colouring of $\{1,\dots,N\}$ contains a monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progression. Classical lower bounds are exponential: Berlekamp gave $W(p+1)>p2^p$ for primes $p$, and the local lemma gives roughly $2^k/k$. Erdos asked whether the growth is in fact superexponential: is it true that $W(k)^{1/k}\to\infty$?
problems.posedBy: Paul Erdos
problems.ageNote: Erdos, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory, Ann. Discrete Math. 6 (1980), p. 90, item (2), as cited by the manuscript. Recorded as Erdos Problem 138, whose companion question $W(k+1)-W(k)\to\infty$ is already in the catalog.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: there is an absolute $K_0$ with $W_r(k)>k^{ck\lfloor\log_2 r\rfloor}$, $c=10^{-5}$, for all $k\ge K_0$ and $r\ge2$; hence $W_r(k)^{1/k}\to\infty$ for each fixed $r$. Prior work in 2026: Fox-Hunter proved superexponential growth for three colours, and Campos-Fox-Schildkraut proved $W_2(k)\ge(1-o(1))k2^{k-1}$, settling $W_2(k)/2^k\to\infty$ but not the limit asked here. Not shown: the companion question $W(k+1)-W(k)\to\infty$, or any upper bound improvement.

problems.name: The classification problem for finite Euclidean Ramsey sets
problems.statement: A finite set $A$ in Euclidean space is Ramsey if for every number of colors $r$ there is a dimension $D$ such that every $r$-coloring of $\mathbb R^D$, with no regularity assumed, contains a monochromatic congruent copy of $A$ at its original scale. Erdos, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus introduced the notion in 1973 and proved that every Ramsey set is spherical. Known Ramsey sets include nondegenerate simplices (Frankl-Rodl), sets with a soluble transitive isometry group and cyclic trapezoids (Kriz), and vertex sets of regular polytopes (Cantwell). Graham conjectured that every spherical set is Ramsey (1994); Leader, Russell and Walters conjectured that a set is Ramsey exactly when it embeds in a finite transitive set (2012). Which finite sets are Ramsey: is there a necessary and sufficient criterion?
problems.posedBy: Erdos, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus, Euclidean Ramsey theorems I, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 14 (1973)
problems.ageNote: The manuscript frames the characterization as the problem of the area since the 1973 paper, with two conjectured answers: Graham's (1994, sphericity) and Leader-Russell-Walters' (2012, subtransitivity). It does not quote an explicit question from the 1973 paper. Graham's conjecture was disproved by Palvolgyi in September 2026, before this manuscript.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: a finite $A\subset\mathbb R^d$ of at least two points with full affine span is Ramsey iff some $(d+1)\times(d+1)$ matrix $P$ over $F\otimes_{\mathbb Q}F$, with $F$ the field generated by the coordinates, satisfies $(p_i\otimes1)^TP(1\otimes p_i)=0$ for every $p_i=(1,a_i)$ and $m_F(P_{\alpha\beta})=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ on the spatial block. Consequences: every subtransitive set and every set of at most five points on a circle is Ramsey; nine circle points with algebraically independent parameters, and twelve points forming three rotated squares, are not. The criterion is exact algebra over the coordinate field; the paper says it is not a procedure for deciding the property from numerical coordinates. The Leader-Russell-Walters disproof is a separate entry. Graham's spherical conjecture had already fallen to Palvolgyi's ChatGPT-found seven-point circle set (arXiv:2609.23327), which this manuscript cites; see graham-spherical-ramsey-conjecture.

problems.name: Yau's nodal-set conjecture for smooth metrics: is nodal measure comparable to sqrt(lambda)?
problems.field: Spectral geometry; nodal sets of Laplace eigenfunctions
problems.statement: Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth closed connected Riemannian manifold of dimension $n$ and $u$ a real eigenfunction, $-\Delta_gu=\lambda u$ with $\lambda>0$. Yau (1982) conjectured that the nodal set $Z_u$ satisfies $c_g\sqrt\lambda\le\mathcal H^{n-1}(Z_u)\le C_g\sqrt\lambda$ with constants depending only on $(M,g)$. Donnelly and Fefferman proved both bounds for real-analytic metrics. For smooth metrics Logunov proved the lower bound in every dimension and a polynomial upper bound; on smooth surfaces the best upper bound was $C\lambda^{3/4-\beta}$ (Logunov-Malinnikova). Does the two-sided bound $\mathcal H^{n-1}(Z_u)\asymp\sqrt\lambda$ hold for every smooth metric, in particular the upper bound?
problems.posedBy: Shing-Tung Yau
problems.ageNote: Yau, Problem section, in Seminar on Differential Geometry, Annals of Mathematics Studies 102 (Princeton, 1982), pp. 669-706, cited by all three manuscripts.
problems.resultNote: Dimensions three and four (Theorems 1.1, 1.2 of the principal manuscript): a smooth metric arbitrarily close to the round metric on $S^3$, and one on $S^2\times T^2$, with exact eigenfunctions whose nodal measure divided by $\sqrt\lambda$ is unbounded. Dimension five and up (companion): a metric on $S^4\times S^1$ with nodal measure $\gg\lambda^{1/2+\epsilon_0}$ for a fixed $\epsilon_0>0$, and products give every dimension above five. Surfaces (companion): $\mathcal H^1(Z_u)\le C(M,g)\sqrt\lambda$, so with Bruning's lower bound Yau's conjecture holds in dimension two. So the upper bound is true for surfaces and false for smooth metrics in every dimension $\ge3$; the lower bound (Logunov) is untouched, and real-analytic metrics are unaffected. No power excess is claimed in dimensions 3 and 4.

problems.name: Naor's question: does nontrivial Markov type force an equivalent uniformly smooth norm (superreflexivity)?
problems.field: Banach space geometry; Ribe program; metric invariants
problems.statement: A normed space $X$ has Markov type $p$ with constant $K$ if for every finite stationary reversible Markov chain $(Z_t)$ on a set $S$, every $f:S\to X$ and every $t\ge1$, $\mathbb E\|f(Z_t)-f(Z_0)\|^p\le K^p\,t\,\mathbb E\|f(Z_1)-f(Z_0)\|^p$. Ball introduced Markov type for Lipschitz extension. Naor, Peres, Schramm and Sheffield showed that uniform smoothness of power type $p$ implies Markov type $p$, so by Pisier's renorming every superreflexive space has Markov type $p$ for some $p>1$. Markov type is a metric property, so a converse would give a metric characterization of superreflexivity in the Ribe program. Naor (2012, Question 4) asked: can a Banach space have nontrivial Markov type (Markov type $p$ for some $p>1$) without admitting an equivalent uniformly smooth norm?
problems.posedBy: Assaf Naor, An introduction to the Ribe program, Japanese Journal of Mathematics 7 (2012), Question 4
problems.resultNote: Claims that every real Banach space with Markov type $p$ for at least one $p>1$ admits an equivalent uniformly convex norm, hence is superreflexive and (by Pisier) admits an equivalent uniformly smooth norm. With the known converse (Naor-Peres-Schramm-Sheffield plus Pisier) this characterizes superreflexivity by nontrivial Markov type, answering Naor's question negatively. The proof builds, from a nonreflexive space finitely representable in a non-superreflexive one, a spreading norm and explicit reversible walks whose image has linear displacement. It does NOT address complex scalars separately, the exact Markov type exponent of a given space, or Ball's Markov type 2 questions for specific spaces.

problems.name: Smooth isometric immersion of every closed Riemannian surface into R^4
problems.statement: Nash's theorem places a compact Riemannian $n$-manifold smoothly and isometrically in Euclidean space of high dimension (17 for surfaces), and Gromov's methods give smooth isometric immersions of closed surfaces into $\mathbb R^5$. In $\mathbb R^3$ the topology and curvature obstruct global immersion and even local smooth immersion is delicate; $C^1$ immersions exist by Nash-Kuiper, and Poznyak treated compact planar domains in $\mathbb R^4$. Gromov recorded the question of smooth isometric immersion of arbitrary Riemannian surfaces into $\mathbb R^4$ (2000) and later attributed it to Chern around 1950. Does every closed smooth Riemannian surface, orientable or not and of any curvature, admit a $C^\infty$ isometric immersion into $\mathbb R^4$?
problems.posedBy: Mikhael Gromov (attributing the question to Shiing-Shen Chern)
problems.ageNote: Gromov, Spaces and questions, GAFA Special Volume (2000), Section I Remark (d). In a 2015 manuscript Gromov attributed the four-space surface question to Chern around 1950, while expressing uncertainty about the compactness qualification.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: every closed smooth Riemannian surface (compact, without boundary, not necessarily orientable or connected, any Gaussian curvature) admits a $C^\infty$ isometric immersion into $\mathbb R^4$; self-intersections are allowed. This lowers Gromov's $\mathbb R^5$ immersion dimension for closed surfaces to four. Not shown: embeddings, noncompact or bounded surfaces (the paper says it treats the compact boundaryless case of Gromov's question), or analytic regularity.

problems.name: The Gromov-Lawson conjecture: closed aspherical manifolds admit no metric of positive scalar curvature
problems.statement: A closed manifold is aspherical if its universal cover is contractible. Gromov and Lawson (1983), with Dirac-operator methods, and Schoen and Yau, with minimal hypersurfaces, obstructed positive scalar curvature on tori and enlargeable manifolds; the conjecture that no closed aspherical manifold carries a metric of positive scalar curvature was open beyond dimension five (Chodosh-Li, Gromov). Hanke (2011, Conjecture 2.9) formulated the stronger homological form: if a closed oriented $n$-manifold $M$ admits positive scalar curvature, the classifying map sends its rational fundamental class to zero in $H_n(B\pi_1(M);\mathbb Q)$. Does any closed aspherical manifold admit a metric of positive scalar curvature, and are positive-scalar-curvature manifolds always rationally inessential?
problems.posedBy: M. Gromov and H. B. Lawson, Positive scalar curvature and the Dirac operator on complete Riemannian manifolds, Publ. Math. IHES 58 (1983); homological form: B. Hanke (2011), Conjecture 2.9
problems.ageNote: The manuscript cites Gromov-Lawson 1983 for the obstruction programme and names the corollary the Gromov-Lawson aspherical conjecture; the homological form is Hanke 2011, Conjecture 2.9, also stated by Yau (2000) and Gromov (2023).
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: if a closed connected oriented smooth $M^n$, $n\ge2$, admits positive scalar curvature then $(c_M)_*[M]=0$ in $H_n(B\pi_1(M);\mathbb Q)$. Corollaries: no closed aspherical manifold (orientable or not) admits positive scalar curvature; every nonnegative-scalar-curvature metric on a closed aspherical manifold is flat; a closed oriented manifold mapping with nonzero degree to an aspherical one has no positive scalar curvature; and nonnegative scalar curvature forces zero real simplicial volume. Prior cases: dimensions 4 and 5 (Chodosh-Li, Gromov). It does not give the quantitative scalar-curvature/simplicial-volume inequality (that is the companion entry).

problems.name: Simon's Problem 1: absolutely continuous spectrum for the weakly disordered Anderson model in dimension three and higher
problems.statement: Let $H_\lambda=-\Delta+\lambda V$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^d)$ with iid site potentials $V_x$ uniform on $[-1,1]$. Anderson (1958) predicted localization at strong disorder; physics predicts that for $d\ge 3$ and weak disorder extended states survive. Absolutely continuous spectrum was proved on the Bethe lattice and on trees (Klein, Aizenman-Sims-Warzel, Aizenman-Warzel), but never on $\mathbb{Z}^d$. Simon's Problem 1 asks: for $d\ge 3$ and suitable small disorder, does $H_\lambda$ almost surely have an energy range of purely absolutely continuous spectrum?
problems.posedBy: Barry Simon (Problem 1 in 'Schrodinger operators in the twenty-first century'), formalizing the extended-states prediction going back to Anderson
problems.ageNote: The physical prediction goes back to Anderson (1958); 2000 is Simon's formulation, which the manuscript cites as the problem.
problems.resultNote: For each $d\ge 3$ there is $\lambda_d>0$ such that for every $0<\lambda<\lambda_d$, almost surely a fixed open interval $I_d$ near the bottom band edge (for $d\ge 4$, $-2d+(1/200,1/100)$) lies in the spectrum and the spectral restriction to $I_d$ is purely absolutely continuous and nonzero. $I_d$ does not depend on $\lambda$. Not shown: a.c. spectrum in the bulk of the band, the location of a mobility edge, quantum diffusion, uniformity in $d$, or other laws.

problems.name: The Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture
problems.field: Geometric group theory; cohomological and geometric dimension of groups
problems.statement: For a group $G$, the cohomological dimension $\mathrm{cd}\,G$ is the projective dimension of the trivial $\mathbb Z[G]$-module $\mathbb Z$, and the geometric dimension $\mathrm{gd}\,G$ is the least dimension of a $K(G,1)$ CW complex; always $\mathrm{cd}\,G\le\mathrm{gd}\,G$. Eilenberg and Ganea (1957) proved $\mathrm{cd}\,G=\mathrm{gd}\,G$ whenever $\mathrm{cd}\,G\ge3$, and Stallings and Swan settled dimension one. Bestvina and Brady (1997) showed that at least one of the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture and Whitehead's asphericity conjecture is false, without deciding which. Does every group of cohomological dimension two admit a two-dimensional classifying space?
problems.posedBy: Samuel Eilenberg and Tudor Ganea, On the Lusternik-Schnirelmann category of abstract groups, Ann. of Math. 65 (1957)
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: there is a finitely generated residually finite group $G$ with $\mathrm{cd}\,G=2$ and $\mathrm{gd}\,G=3$; no two-dimensional $K(G,1)$ exists regardless of the number of cells. $G$ is a Bestvina-Brady group (the kernel of the height map of a right-angled Artin group); it is of type FL and FP$_\infty$ but not finitely presented. The obstruction compares an acyclic two-dimensional level complex with any hypothetical aspherical presentation, using small SU(2) labelings and a degree argument. It does not give a finitely presented counterexample, and by itself it does not decide Whitehead's asphericity conjecture.

problems.name: Erdős Problem #3: sets with divergent reciprocal sum contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions
problems.statement: If $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ satisfies $\sum_{n\in A}1/n=\infty$, must $A$ contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions? This extends Szemeredi's theorem to sparse sets, including the primes. The case of three-term progressions was settled by Bloom and Sisask (2020); for general $k$ the best bound before this work, $r_k(N)\ll_kN\exp(-(\log\log N)^{c_k})$ of Leng, Sah and Sawhney, falls short of the summability over dyadic intervals that the conjecture needs, where $r_k(N)$ is the largest size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no $k$-term progression. Does every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contain $k$-term arithmetic progressions for every $k$?
problems.posedBy: Paul Erdős
problems.ageNote: The manuscript cites Erdos, Problems, Math. Balkanica 4 (1974), Problem 4.33.6. The density version goes back to Erdos and Turan (1936), and the problem is often called the Erdos-Turan conjecture on arithmetic progressions; erdosproblems.com lists it as Problem #3 with a 5000 dollar prize.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1 claims, for each fixed $k\ge3$, $r_k(N)\le C_kN\exp(-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k})$ with unspecified positive constants depending on $k$; equivalently a density-$\alpha$ subset of $[N]$ has a $k$-term progression once $\log N\ge A_k(2+\log(1/\alpha))^{A_k}$. Summing over dyadic blocks gives Erdos's conjecture, and even the stronger criterion with weights $(\log(2+a))^B/a$, and recovers Green-Tao for dense subsets of the primes. The method is a density increment on triangular polynomial cells with controlled precision. No improvement of the three-term exponent is claimed, the exponents $\varepsilon_k$ are not optimized, and it does not give an asymptotic formula for $r_k(N)$ (Erdos Problem #142).

problems.name: Gyarfas's conjecture on covering edge-colored complete graphs by r-1 monochromatic trees
problems.statement: Color each edge of a finite complete graph with one of $r$ colors. A monochromatic tree cover is a family of monochromatic trees (overlaps and single vertices allowed) whose vertex sets cover the graph. The $r$ monochromatic stars at any vertex always give a cover by $r$ trees. Gyarfas conjectured that $r-1$ trees always suffice; Erdos, Gyarfas and Pyber recorded that this covering formulation is equivalent to the intersecting case of Ryser's conjecture. Can the vertices of every $r$-edge-colored complete graph be covered by at most $r-1$ monochromatic trees?
problems.posedBy: Andras Gyarfas; recorded by Erdos, Gyarfas and Pyber (J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 51, 1991)
problems.ageNote: The manuscripts cite Erdos-Gyarfas-Pyber (1991, Section 3) and Milicevic (2017, Conjecture 1); they give no earlier source, so 1991 is the earliest date the literature here supports.
problems.resultNote: For every sufficiently large prime $q$ (September 27 paper), and for $r=s^n+1$ with $s\equiv2\pmod3$ a large prime and $n$ large odd (September 23 paper), there is a finite complete graph with an $r$-edge-coloring whose vertices need exactly $r$ monochromatic trees to cover them; the same holds for connected monochromatic subgraphs. Built from the Ryser counterexamples by coloring each pair of hyperedges by a part where they meet. Not addressed: small $r$, or the distinct vertex-disjoint tree-partition conjecture of Erdos-Gyarfas-Pyber.

problems.name: Smith-Toda complexes V(n) at every height when the prime may vary
problems.statement: At a prime $p$, a Smith-Toda complex $V(n)$ is a finite $p$-local spectrum whose Brown-Peterson homology is $BP_*/(p,v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ as a $BP_*BP$-comodule, each generator killed to its first power. Adams, Smith and Toda constructed $V(1)$, $V(2)$, $V(3)$ for $p>2,4,6$; Nave proved that $V((p+1)/2)$ does not exist for $p\ge7$; and Culver-Zhang (2023 version) recorded the existence of $V(4)$ as open at every prime. Hopkins-Smith periodicity realizes suitable higher powers, not first powers. The Smith-Toda realization problem asks for which $n$ and $p$ the complex $V(n)$ exists. For every height $n$, does $V(n)$ exist at some prime $p$?
problems.posedBy: The Smith-Toda realization problem (Smith 1970, Toda 1971); V(4) recorded open by Culver and Zhang (2023 arXiv version)
problems.ageNote: The manuscript frames this as the Smith-Toda realization problem, citing Smith (1970) and Toda (1971), and does not name a poser for the all-height, varying-prime form; 1971 is the date of Toda's paper. The V(4) record is from the September 2023 version of Culver-Zhang.
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: for every $n\ge0$ there are a prime $p$ and a finite $p$-local spectrum $X$ with $BP_*X\cong BP_*/(p,v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ as comodules with the canonical coaction and generator in degree zero. The companion constructs $V(4)$ at $p=1009$, answering the existence question Culver-Zhang recorded as open at every prime. Partial for the realization problem: no explicit or effective prime for $n\ge5$, no statement that $V(n)$ exists for all large $p$, no multiplicative structure, and nothing on the gap between Nave's nonexistence range and the constructed cases.

problems.name: The circulant Hadamard conjecture: real circulant Hadamard matrices exist only in orders 1 and 4
problems.field: Design theory; Hadamard matrices and difference sets
problems.statement: A real Hadamard matrix of order $n$ is an $n\times n$ matrix $H$ with entries $\pm1$ and $HH^T=nI_n$; it is circulant if every row is the cyclic shift of the first. Order 4 has the example with first row $(-1,1,1,1)$, and order 1 is trivial. The circulant Hadamard conjecture, traditionally attributed to Ryser (1963), asserts that there are no others. Turyn showed any further order is $4u^2$ with $u$ odd and not a prime power; field descent and later methods of Schmidt and Leung-Schmidt, and the 2017 computation of Logan and Mossinghoff, excluded all but 4489 orders up to $4\cdot10^{30}$. Several claimed proofs have appeared. Is every real circulant Hadamard matrix of order 1 or 4?
problems.posedBy: Herbert J. Ryser (traditional attribution)
problems.ageNote: The manuscript says the conjecture is traditionally attributed to Ryser and cites his Carus monograph Combinatorial Mathematics (1963) and Leung-Schmidt (2012).
problems.resultNote: Theorem 1.1: a real circulant Hadamard matrix of order $n\ge1$ exists if and only if $n\in\{1,4\}$. Section 2 reproves Turyn's restriction $n=4u^2$ with $u$ odd, and the main argument excludes every odd $u>1$ through an alternating product of character values over the primes dividing $u$. Corollary 1.2 deduces the Barker-sequence classification. It says nothing about the (non-circulant) Hadamard conjecture on existence in every order divisible by 4, nor about complex or group-developed variants.
